# Legacy Sunset & Migration Program — Second Consultation Draft

*How this document is meant to be read.* This is a revision, and it exists because colleagues were generous enough to press hard on the first version. Where the criticism was right — and it mostly was — I have changed the plan rather than defended it. Where I have kept a position, I have tried to say why, and to leave it open for the room to settle.

Two requests before the content. First, the numbers below are **placeholders, deliberately visible so that Finance can correct them** — they are offered as a starting shape, not as positions I hold. Second, I would prefer this circulate to Finance, Legal, Field Leadership and the legacy engineering elders *before* it reaches the leadership meeting, so that by the time it is discussed formally, no one is hearing anything for the first time and no one is put in the position of having to disagree in front of others.

There are now **three gates**. Everything else can proceed quietly in parallel and be adjusted.

---

## 1. What this program is actually about

Not decommissioning. We are transferring a third of our profit from one platform to another *without the customer feeling transferred*, while defusing two slow-burning hazards: unpatched surface area, and institutional memory walking out the door.

Three framing observations carried forward from the first draft, because they survived scrutiny:

- **The announcement is the single largest defection event in the program.** The day we publish a date, procurement at every large account is handed a legitimate reason to run a competitive evaluation. Sequence matters more than timeline.
- **A published date that slips is worse than a longer date held.** Credibility is the currency we are spending.
- **Tooling retains customers; discounts only renew them.** Fear is the real churn driver, and fear responds to demonstrable safety, not to price.

And one correction I now accept as the most important criticism of the first draft: **the previous version was a strategy memo wearing a program plan's clothes.** It had no money in it. That is fixed below, and the financial work now sits *ahead* of the timeline, not behind it.

---

## 2. The financial spine (new — and now the first gate, not an appendix)

The brief says a third of **profit**. The first draft set a target on **revenue**. Those are not the same thing, and the gap between them is the entire problem.

### 2.1 The profit bridge

Illustrative, indexed so the shape is arguable even before Finance supplies real figures. Let legacy annual revenue = **100**.

| | Legacy today | Same customer, migrated, flat revenue |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 100 | 100 |
| Cost of delivery | −15 (frozen, on-prem, no hosting) | −25 (hosting, higher support surface) |
| R&D allocation | −3 (development stopped years ago) | −15 (active roadmap) |
| Migration cost, amortised over 3y | 0 | −8 |
| **Contribution** | **≈82** | **≈52** |

The uncomfortable implication, which I would rather we all look at together now than discover at Gate 2: **at 100% customer retention and flat pricing, we lose roughly a third of the contribution this base produces.** Legacy profit is high precisely because we stopped investing. Migration re-imposes the investment.

Therefore the program's success measure changes:

- **Old target:** ≥90% of legacy revenue retained through EOL.
- **Revised target:** ≥90% of legacy revenue retained **and** ≥80% of legacy contribution held at T0+48, recovering to ≥100% by T0+60 through expansion — which requires **net +12–18% price/scope realisation on migration**, delivered through consolidation and upsell rather than list-price increases.

That last clause is the real design constraint on the incentive schemes in §8. Any incentive that structurally forecloses expansion is, on these numbers, a decision to permanently shrink our profit base.

### 2.2 Perpetual-to-subscription conversion (previously absent, and material)

If the legacy base is perpetual-licence-plus-maintenance and the replacement is subscription, we face a **recognised-revenue cliff and a cash trough that occur even at zero churn**. This is not a churn story; it is an accounting and guidance story.

- Model the transition in ratable terms before any date is published.
- Offer **prepaid multi-year subscription** and, where the customer's own capex cycle demands it, a **term-licence bridge** on the new platform, so the customer's procurement model does not become a migration blocker.
- If we are publicly reporting: this is a guidance event. Legal, Finance and IR must be satisfied *before* T0, and the announcement is better placed on or near a scheduled results cycle than dropped between them.

### 2.3 Three paths, priced against each other (Gate 0 deliverable)

We should not choose the migration path by default. The baseline for comparison is **harvest**, not migrate.

| Path | Description | Illustrative shape |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Migrate & convert** | Program as described here | ~55–70% of one year's legacy revenue in total program spend over 4 years; profit trough T0+15 to T0+27; strongest long-term position |
| **B — Harvest at premium** | No parity rebuild, minimal tooling, stepped maintenance uplift, accept 25–40% attrition, EOL at T0+36 | Highest near-term cash, lowest capability, highest relationship damage. **This is the financial baseline every other path must beat.** |
| **C — Divest / carve-out** | Sell or spin the legacy line to a long-tail maintenance specialist | Removes cost curve, monetises tail, serves the most bespoke customers better than we intend to. Partly *mutually exclusive* with A: funding Tier A customers off the platform destroys the asset |
| **C′ — Third-party maintenance partnership** | Retain ownership and customers; contract a specialist firm for sustaining engineering and security | Solves the retirement constraint without divesting. **Strongly recommended as a component of A regardless of path choice** |

**Owner:** CFO with Corporate Development, supported by the program lead.
**Decision forced at Gate 0 (Month 3), not left to drift.** The first draft raised divestiture twice and then orphaned it; that was a way of avoiding a hard conversation, and I should not have done it.

**Quantified trigger:** if the irreducible bespoke core (from §5 triage) exceeds **25% of legacy revenue and is concentrated in fewer than 12 accounts**, or if parity rebuild cost exceeds **1.5× the NPV of retained contribution**, we open a divestiture process for that segment. We run A and C on a dual track until Gate 0 and we do not spend Tier A migration money before that gate closes.

**Program budget cap:** proposed at ≈65% of one year of legacy revenue over four years, with a 15% contingency reserve released only by the steering group. A cap that no one may quietly exceed is kinder to everyone than a budget that is renegotiated in twelve separate conversations.

---

## 3. Two gating questions that must be answered before any date is published

The first draft presented a timeline as settled while two of its preconditions were still Phase 0 tasks. That was inconsistent, and the criticism is accepted.

### 3.1 Deployment-model compatibility (the omission I am most embarrassed by)

If the legacy product is self-managed and the replacement is SaaS-only, then **architecture, not features, is the blocker** for exactly the accounts most likely to defect: data residency, air-gapped or classified environments, regulated sectors with cloud prohibitions, customers whose own compliance regime forbids multi-tenancy. No amount of parity engineering or dual-run tooling solves this.

**Month 1–3 task, before anything else:** quantify legacy revenue sitting in cloud-prohibited or residency-constrained environments. Then a decision at Gate 0 from three options:

1. Fund a **self-managed / sovereign edition** of the new product (expensive, slow, strategically significant — properly a leadership decision, not a program decision).
2. Offer **single-tenant dedicated hosting** in-region as a narrower answer.
3. Classify these accounts as **structurally non-migratable** and route them to path C or C′, with the relationship handled as a deliberate, respectful handover rather than a failure.

If the answer is (1), the timeline in §7 lengthens and I would rather say so now.

### 3.2 Contract archaeology as a *precondition* to the date

The top 50 legacy contracts must be read before T0, hunting for perpetual grants, evergreen support obligations, uptime/patch commitments, source escrow, public-sector and regulated terms, and notice periods.

- The announced timeline is **explicitly conditional** on this review. If perpetual or evergreen rights exist, T0+48 is legally hollow for those accounts and pretending otherwise invites a dispute that would damage far more than the program.
- Where such rights exist, we prepare a **waiver-for-consideration mechanism**: migration funded, price locked, credits granted, in exchange for a documented release of the perpetual entitlement.
- **Source escrow requires its own decision.** Mass escrow release at EOL is an IP problem and a gift to any third-party maintainer or competitor. Preferred substitute, offered proactively and warmly: a **supported continuity option** — the binary plus a named third-party maintenance provider under licence — which serves the customer's actual need (continuity) better than source they cannot realistically build.
- Some customers' own audit or certification regimes require a vendor-supported platform. For them, EOL date = the date they fail an audit. They need earlier engagement and, in some cases, path C′.

---

## 4. Phase 0 — quiet internal work (Months 0–9)

A distinction the first draft blurred: **internal preparation may take nine months; the window of selective external disclosure may not.** Nine months of internal work is prudent. Nine months of privately telling twenty large customers something the rest of the market does not know is a leak, a fairness problem, and possibly a disclosure problem. Corrected in §11.

**Evidence gathering without touching the platform.** "Freeze and harden" and "ship telemetry" contradicted each other, and many customers would refuse the telemetry build anyway. Revised evidence hierarchy, in order of reliance:

1. **Licence-key / entitlement data** — what was purchased and enabled (available now, no build).
2. **Configuration and schema dumps** collected through routine support channels.
3. **Five years of support tickets**, mined for feature mentions.
4. **Structured interviews** with the top 50 accounts' administrators — not sales conversations, technical ones.
5. **Optional telemetry**, offered as an opt-in diagnostic bundle to willing customers only, never as a forced upgrade.

**On the annual-cycle blind spot** — this criticism changed a decision. A six-month observation window will confidently retire a year-end close, statutory report, annual audit export or seasonal batch job, and break a strategic account in month 20. Therefore:

- Cycle-sensitive subsystems (financial close, statutory/regulatory reporting, archival export, scheduled batch) are **exempt from usage-based retirement**. For these, interview and contract evidence outrank telemetry, and the default is *retain or bridge* until positively disproven.
- We commit to observing **at least one full annual cycle** before any cycle-sensitive capability is placed in the retire bucket, even if that means a subset of triage decisions closes at Gate 2 rather than Gate 1.

**Knowledge capture, treated as urgent rather than important.** Retention agreements with the handful of engineers who genuinely hold the model, structured against *deliverables* — recorded architecture walkthroughs, runbooks, failure catalogues, a named and demonstrably competent successor. Pairing rotation. Contractor bench engaged warm. **Bus factor ≥3 per critical subsystem by T0+12, tracked as a program metric with a target.**

**Freeze and harden.** Encapsulate the stack, modern gateway and WAF in front, narrow the network surface, move authentication to the current identity layer, reduce the patch obligation to the smallest defensible set. This converts an open-ended liability into something close to a fixed-cost appliance.

**Third-party maintenance partner selected and contracted by T0+6.** This is the answer to a contradiction the first draft left standing (see §7).

---

## 5. Feature triage — rebuild versus retire

A rule, so the argument happens once and no one has to lose it repeatedly in public.

Score each legacy-only capability on (a) revenue-weighted adoption, (b) existence of a workflow substitute, (c) strategic coherence with the new product, (d) rebuild cost, (e) **cycle sensitivity** (new).

| Bucket | Criteria | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Rebuild native** | >15% of legacy revenue, or ≥3 strategic accounts, and consistent with product direction | First-class implementation: dated, funded, on the roadmap |
| **Rebuild as compatibility layer** | Behaviour-bound rather than value-bound — exact semantics matter (report formats, macro syntax, obscure protocols, batch quirks) | Adapter/shim, explicitly labelled a compatibility surface with its own later sunset. Contain the ugliness |
| **Partner or services** | Genuinely bespoke, one or two accounts, high cost, low fit | Partner/SI delivery, funded custom extension, or licensed module. Candidate for path C |
| **Retire with a landing** | Trivial usage, superior path exists, and **not cycle-sensitive** | Retire — never bare. Documented alternative, hands-on transition session, commercial gesture where appropriate |
| **Archive** *(new)* | Needed only for records retention, not operations | **Read-only archival edition** — see §10 |

Nothing enters "retire" without a named alternative and a named human who has walked a real customer through it.

---

## 6. Parity control regime (new — the largest structural gap in the first draft)

The first draft named parity-list growth as the most likely failure mode and then provided no control for it. That was a real omission.

- **Per-account parity freeze:** the list closes **60 days after that account's assessment**, in writing, signed by both sides. Items raised later are handled through change control, not absorbed silently.
- **Fixed parity engineering budget** = 12% of program spend, plus a 20% reserve released only by the steering group.
- **One-in-one-out:** after freeze, a new parity item is accepted only by displacing one of equal or greater effort, chosen with the customer. This makes the trade-off visible and shared rather than adversarial.
- **Named escalation owner:** Product Lead and Program Lead jointly, single decision, 5-day turnaround.
- **Leading indicator with a threshold:** new parity items opened per account per month. Sustained above 1.5 for two consecutive months triggers an out-of-cyc

We do not have a returns *processing* problem. We have a **demand-quality problem with a logistics symptom, and an inventory-decay problem with an accounting symptom.**

- **The queue is not the cost. The clock is.** A returned unit is not a cost centre; it is depreciating inventory sitting in a room where nobody has been given the authority to decide its fate today. Most of the value destruction happens between the dock and the decision, not in the labour of touching the item.
- **A return rate target, on its own, is a demand-suppression target.** If we measure the team on return rate and nothing else, the fastest path to green is to sell less, to sell more conservatively, and to make returning unpleasant. Customer research is already telling us where that road ends. So the north-star metric has to be a *contribution* metric, and the return rate has to sit underneath it as a diagnostic.
- **Customers who return are not the problem cohort; they are frequently the best cohort.** In most catalogues the highest-LTV segment returns above average, because they buy more and buy more experimentally. A very small cohort is genuinely abusive. Conflating the two is how retailers accidentally fire their best customers. Differentiated, evidence-based treatment — invisible to the 97% — rather than policy change applied to everyone.

And the criticism I would make of the way this problem is usually presented internally: **"tighten the policy" and "absorb the cost" are presented as the only two options because the third option is unglamorous.** The third option is that a large share of these returns are *manufactured by us* — by thin product content, drifting vendor sizing, pick errors, damage in transit, and promise dates we miss. Those returns are free to fix, in the sense that fixing them costs content and QC effort rather than margin.

This needs an explicit split: recovery credited at retail only where the unit sells into **incremental** demand (out-of-stock backfill, outlet channel with distinct buyers), otherwise at COGS avoided.

**5. The 6-point prevention improvement is asserted, not derived.** There is no decomposition of the 28% into fit/size, not-as-described, defective, wrong item, damaged in transit, late delivery, buyer's remorse, bracketing, wardrobing — with an addressable share and an intervention against each. **6. The $10.50 → $7.00 handling target is unmodelled and implausible as constructed.** Return freight ($3.85) is the largest line and the redesign says nothing about freight (drop-off, consolidation, carrier mix, label-less returns).
